With her new home, Ruiz will be able to continue -- and even expand -- her family's work for those in need. According to Executive Producer Anthony Dominici, both an additional kitchen and storage space were built in the new home for Ruiz. And "through the generosity of the community," enough donations of food, clothes and toys were collected to fill a 20-foot shipping container and a 16-foot cube truck -- including more than 75,000 cans of food, Dominici said. "That's the whole point here," Pennington said. "To give her what she needs to make her life easier to literally spread dreams and hope to people who have absolutely none of either one of those." For Ruiz, it's about teaching young minds so they can in turn give back to their community. "If you teach them and train them as a child and they go out and do the same, we would live in a much better world." Actress Selena Gomez introduced and presented Ruiz with her CNN Hero award. Each of the top 10 CNN Heroes also received $25,000.  Watch Ruiz accept her CNN Hero Award » . EL PASO, Texas (CNN) -- For more than 12 years, CNN Hero Maria Ruiz has devoted herself to transforming the lives of children and their families in Juarez, Mexico. Recently, however, it is Ruiz's own life that has undergone a remarkable transformation.

In November, "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" honored Ruiz for crossing the Texas border into Juarez several times each week to deliver food, clothing and toys to impoverished children and their families. Months later, Ruiz and her family were met with yet another surprise, this one courtesy of ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition."

Ruiz, her husband and their two children were sent on a five-day vacation to the Bahamas while thousands of volunteers constructed a custom-designed home for the family.

"When Ty Pennington came to our home and said, 'Ruiz family, come on out,' we all just ran out and couldn't believe that we were chosen," Ruiz said. "It's a blessing to us, but we weren't expecting all of this at all, and it has been overwhelming."

Pennington, the host of "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition," selected Ruiz and her family from among thousands of applicants throughout Texas. His aim, he explained, was to give Ruiz what she needed most: the tools to accomplish even more.

In addition to delivering supplies to the people of Juarez, Ruiz and her family are completing construction of a complex there that will include a community kitchen, an orphanage and a trade school.

In order to dedicate their time to the Juarez community, the family placed the construction of their own home on hold in 1996, Ruiz said, leaving many parts unfinished. Much of their living space, she added, was also being used as a warehouse for the donations intended for the Juarez families.

"A home is somewhere you can go after a long day's work and relax, and where the family can get together and be able to sit down and talk about our day," Ruiz said. "When we had the things in the living room, we couldn't do that there."

Upon returning from the Bahamas, Ruiz and her family were welcomed by thousands of volunteers and community members, while the show's large bus blocked their view of the transformation. After joining in the program's signature chant -- "Move that bus!" -- Ruiz and her family were at last introduced to their new home.

"For us, it is a new beginning, and it's going to change our lives," Ruiz said.

With her new home, Ruiz will be able to continue -- and even expand -- her family's work on behalf of those in need. According to Executive Producer Anthony Dominici, both an additional kitchen and storage space were incorporated into the new home for Ruiz. And "through the generosity of the community," enough donations of food, clothes and toys were collected to fill a 20-foot shipping container and a 16-foot cube truck -- including more than 75,000 cans of food, Dominici said.

"That's the whole point here," Pennington said. "To give her what she needs to make her life easier, to literally spread dreams and hope to people who have absolutely none of either one of those."

For Ruiz, her mission centers on nurturing young minds so that they, in turn, may give back to their community. "If you teach them and train them as a child, and they go out and do the same, we would live in a much better world."

"CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" introduced Ruiz to the world when it premiered on Thanksgiving across the global networks of CNN. Actress Selena Gomez introduced Ruiz and presented her with her CNN Hero award. Each of the top 10 CNN Heroes also received $25,000.

Nominations for the 2009 CNN Heroes opened January 1 and may be submitted at www.CNN.com/Heroes. The Ruiz family episode of "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition" is scheduled to air March 15.

"When Ty Pennington showed up at our house and called out, 'Ruiz family, come on out,' we all rushed outside and simply couldn't believe we'd been picked," Ruiz recalled. "It's a blessing for us, but we had absolutely no idea any of this was coming, and it has been overwhelming."

Pennington, who hosts "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition," explained that Ruiz and her family were chosen out of thousands who applied from across Texas. The goal, according to Pennington, was to provide Ruiz with exactly what she needed most: the resources to accomplish even more.

Beyond delivering goods to Juarez residents, Ruiz and her family are finishing work on a facility there that will house a community kitchen, an orphanage, and a vocational school.

Ruiz explained that in 1996 the family had set aside work on their own house so they could focus on serving the Juarez community, which meant numerous sections remained incomplete. On top of that, a large portion of their living quarters had become a storage area for all the donated items destined for the Juarez families.

"Home should be the place you return to after a long, hard day to unwind, where the whole family can gather, sit down and share how their day went," Ruiz said. "With all those things piled up in the living room, we simply couldn't do that in there."

When Ruiz and her family came back from the Bahamas, they were greeted by thousands of volunteers and neighbors, while the program's massive bus was positioned to hide the renovations from view. Once everyone shouted the show's signature line -- "Move that bus!" -- Ruiz and her family got their first look at their new home.

"For us, this marks a fresh start, and it's going to transform our lives," Ruiz said.

Dominici added that "through the generosity of the community," donations of food, clothing and toys poured in -- enough to fill a 20-foot shipping container along with a 16-foot cube truck, including over 75,000 cans of food.

"That's really the entire purpose here," Pennington said. "It's about giving her what she needs to make her own life easier so she can genuinely deliver dreams and hope to people who have none of either."

Ruiz was introduced to audiences worldwide through "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute," which debuted on Thanksgiving across CNN's global networks. Actress Selena Gomez presented Ruiz with her CNN Hero award. All 10 of the top CNN Heroes were also awarded $25,000 each.

Food, clothing, and toys—items most people take for granted—became lifelines for the impoverished communities Ruiz devoted herself to serving. Her tireless dedication earned her recognition as a CNN Hero, but for years, her own family lived in modest circumstances, their house perpetually unfinished as Ruiz prioritized the needs of others over her own comfort.

Much of the Ruiz home had been transformed into something more like a warehouse than a residence. Rooms that might have offered space for family life were instead packed with donations awaiting delivery across the border. The unfinished house stood as a testament to Ruiz's selflessness—every resource, every square foot, dedicated to her charitable work rather than to creating a comfortable home for herself and her loved ones.

That changed when Ruiz was selected from among thousands of applicants for ABC's beloved reality series "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition." The show, known for transforming the lives of deserving families through remarkable home renovations, recognized in Ruiz exactly the kind of person its mission was designed to celebrate. While she and her family enjoyed a well-deserved vacation in the Bahamas, the show's team set to work building them a custom home from the ground up.

The new residence was more than just a place to live—it was a foundation for everything Ruiz hoped to accomplish. For the first time, her family had a proper space to call their own, a true home rather than a storage facility for donations. But the transformation extended far beyond personal comfort. The project provided Ruiz with the tools and infrastructure to dramatically expand her charitable work.

Among the additions was a community complex designed to multiply her impact across the border. The complex featured a kitchen to prepare and provide meals, an orphanage to shelter children in need, and a trade school to offer education and practical skills that could help lift families out of poverty for generations. In building Maria Ruiz a home, "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition" had done something greater still—it had empowered a woman whose life's work was giving to others, ensuring that her extraordinary generosity could reach even further into the communities she had spent over a decade serving.

For years, Maria Ruiz has crossed the border between El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, carrying food, clothing, and hope to children living in one of the region's most impoverished communities. Now, the woman who has given so much to others is receiving a life-changing gift of her own.

The popular television program, known for transforming the lives of deserving families and community heroes, selected Ruiz for her extraordinary commitment to helping others.

The surprise left the humble humanitarian overwhelmed with emotion. For someone who has spent years focused entirely on the needs of others, receiving such a gift proved to be a deeply moving experience.

# Volunteer Who Spent Years Aiding Migrants Receives Surprise Home Makeover

*A community rallies to give back to a woman who gave so much to others*

For more than a decade, Maria Delgado's own home fell into quiet disrepair while she poured her time, energy, and modest savings into helping others.

The 58-year-old retired schoolteacher has become a familiar figure along the stretch of borderland where she lives, spending her mornings preparing meals, organizing donated clothing, and offering water and first aid to weary travelers. She never asked for recognition—only that people be treated with dignity.

"I always tell them, 'You are not a burden. You are a person,'" Delgado said, her voice steady but soft. "That's all anyone wants to hear."

## A House That Told a Story of Sacrifice

Neighbors say Delgado's dedication came at a personal cost. Her roof had leaked for years. Her kitchen appliances had long since stopped working properly. The paint outside her small stucco home had faded under the relentless desert sun.

"She would give away her last dollar," said longtime friend and fellow volunteer Rosa Jimenez. "She'd fix a stranger's blister before she'd fix her own front door."

That quiet self-sacrifice is what inspired a group of local business owners, contractors, and volunteers to take action.

## The Surprise

Under the guise of attending a "community thank-you luncheon," Delgado was led away from her home for the day. When she returned, more than 40 people had gathered on her street.

The house she left that morning was not the house she came back to.

A new roof gleamed overhead. Fresh paint brightened the exterior. Inside, volunteers had installed a working kitchen, repaired the plumbing, and furnished the living room with donated furniture. A local nursery had even planted a small garden—something Delgado had always wanted but never found time for.

She stood frozen on the sidewalk, hands over her mouth, before tears came.

"I don't have the words," she managed. "I only did what any person should do. This—this is too much."

## A Community Effort

Organizers said the project came together in just three weeks, powered entirely by donated labor and materials.

"Maria has been the heart of this town's kindness for years," said contractor Danny Reyes, who coordinated the renovation. "We couldn't fix the whole world for her, but we could fix her home. It was the least we could do."

Local restaurants provided food for the workers. A hardware store donated supplies at cost. Teenagers from the high school where Delgado once taught showed up to paint and haul debris.

"She taught half this town," Reyes added with a laugh. "You don't say no to Ms. Delgado."

## "I'll Just Keep Going"

Even amid the celebration, Delgado's thoughts returned to the people she serves. When asked what the makeover meant to her, she paused.

"It means I have a warm place to rest now," she said. "And that means I can wake up tomorrow and keep helping. That's what I'll do. I'll just keep going."

As the sun set over her freshly painted home, Delgado was already talking about the next morning's supply run.

Some things, it seems, no makeover could ever change.

---

# Building Bridges: How One Texas Family's Cross-Border Mission Earned National Recognition

*A feature on charity, community, and the transformative power of everyday heroes*

---

In the dusty outskirts of a small town near the Texas-Mexico border, the Reyes family never set out to become national figures. They simply saw a need—and answered it.

For more than a decade, Miguel and Sofia Reyes had been crossing into Mexico most weekends, their pickup truck loaded with lumber, medical supplies, and secondhand clothing. What began as occasional charity runs to a struggling colonia outside Ciudad Juárez evolved into something far larger: a grassroots organization that has helped build dozens of homes for families living in poverty.

## A Convergence of Two American Traditions

Their story caught the attention of producers behind two beloved programs known for celebrating and empowering the extraordinary among us.

*CNN Heroes*, the network's annual tribute to everyday people making a difference, had been tracking nominations for its yearly gala. Meanwhile, *Extreme Makeover: Home Edition*—the emotional powerhouse that rebuilt homes for deserving families—recognized a poetic symmetry: here was a family who had spent years building homes for others, often at the expense of their own aging property back in Texas.

The result was an unprecedented collaboration that honored the Reyes family on both fronts.

## The Work Behind the Recognition

"We're not heroes," Sofia Reyes insisted during filming, her voice catching. "We're just people who couldn't look away."

Their nonprofit, which they run entirely on donations and volunteer labor, has constructed simple but sturdy cinderblock homes for families who previously lived in structures made of scrap wood and tarpaulin. Each home includes something many recipients had never known: a solid roof, secure walls, and a door that locks.

The couple's three children grew up on these job sites, learning to mix concrete before they could drive.

## When the Builders Became the Recipients

In a twist that moved viewers to tears, the *Extreme Makeover* team surprised the Reyes family by renovating their own modest Texas home—one they had neglected for years while pouring resources into their mission. The seven-day rebuild honored their sacrifice while giving them a proper base of operations.

Days later, at the *CNN Heroes* ceremony, Miguel Reyes accepted his award with characteristic humility.

"This isn't about a border," he told the audience. "It's about neighbors. When someone across the river needs help, they're not a stranger. They're family."

## A Lasting Legacy

The dual recognition brought a surge of donations and volunteers to the family's cause, allowing them to expand operations and mentor other cross-border charity groups.

For the Reyes family, the spotlight was fleeting—but the mission continues, one home at a time.

---

*This feature illustrates how humanitarian storytelling can bridge cultures, communities, and even nations.*

# 'Extreme Makeover' Transforms Life of CNN Hero Who Feeds Mexico's Forgotten Children

*Volunteer who spent years delivering food across the border receives dream home in emotional community rebuild*

By Staff Writer

In a tearful reveal that drew hundreds of community members to a quiet neighborhood this weekend, the cast and crew of "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition" unveiled a completely rebuilt home for a local family whose tireless work feeding impoverished children in Mexico earned national recognition as a CNN Hero.

The family, whose modest and deteriorating house had fallen into disrepair after years of pouring their personal resources into their charity work, watched in disbelief as the show's signature bus pulled away to reveal their transformed home.

## A Mission Born from Compassion

For more than a decade, the family has crossed the border multiple times each month, loading trucks with food, clothing, medical supplies, and school materials for children living in extreme poverty in colonias outside Tijuana.

"We started with just our own car and whatever we could afford to buy," the father told reporters at the reveal. "We saw kids who hadn't eaten in days, kids without shoes, families living in conditions no child should ever endure. We couldn't just look away."

Their grassroots operation grew into a lifeline for hundreds of families, delivering thousands of meals annually while operating on a shoestring budget.

## The Personal Cost

That dedication came at a price. The family had deferred nearly all home maintenance for years, redirecting money toward their mission. Their house suffered from a failing roof, faulty plumbing, and structural issues that made daily life a struggle.

"When we learned about what this family had sacrificed—not just their money but their comfort, their own home—to help children they'd never met across the border, we knew we had to be here," said host Ty Pennington, standing before the newly completed house. "These are the people who remind us what it means to be human."

Pennington, known for his boundless energy and emotional connection with families, said this build resonated deeply with the crew.

"You meet a lot of incredible people doing this job," Pennington continued. "But there's something about someone who quietly, without any expectation of recognition, gets up every day to make sure a child hundreds of miles away doesn't go to bed hungry. That's a hero. That's the real deal."

## The Reveal

As the crowd chanted the show's famous "Move that bus!" the family fell to their knees at the sight of their new home—a spacious, fully accessible house complete with a dedicated storage and staging area for their charitable supplies.

"I can't believe this is real," the mother said through tears. "We never asked for anything. We just wanted to help those children. And now... now we have a place where we can do even more."

The build included a specially designed warehouse-style garage where the family can organize donations, plus a commercial-grade refrigeration unit to store perishable food before deliveries.

# Juárez Woman's Decades of Service to the Poor Honored with CNN Hero Award and a New Home

**JUÁREZ, Mexico** — For more than twenty years, Maria Ruiz has walked the dusty streets of Juárez's poorest neighborhoods carrying food, medicine, and something even rarer: unwavering hope. This week, the world finally recognized what her community has known all along. Ruiz was named a CNN Hero, and in a surprise announcement that left her in tears, she was also gifted a brand-new custom-built home.

"I have never done this work for a reward," Ruiz said, her voice trembling as she stood before neighbors and volunteers who had gathered to celebrate. "I did it because these are my people, my family. But God has blessed me beyond anything I could have imagined."

## A Mission Born from Struggle

Ruiz's journey began in the late 1990s, when she was a struggling mother herself, barely able to feed her own children. Rather than allowing hardship to harden her heart, she chose compassion. She began cooking extra meals to share with families even more desperate than her own.

"I remembered what it felt like to have nothing," she recalled. "I couldn't look away from a hungry child when I had even a little to give."

What started as a few shared plates grew into a sprawling grassroots operation. Today, Ruiz runs a community kitchen that feeds hundreds of families each week, along with a small clinic offering basic medical care and a program that provides school supplies to children who might otherwise never attend class.

## Answering the Call in Dangerous Times

Juárez, once labeled one of the most dangerous cities in the world, presented Ruiz with challenges few could imagine. During the height of cartel violence, when many aid workers fled, she stayed.

"People told me I was crazy to keep going out," she said. "But if I stopped, who would help these families? Fear cannot be an excuse when people are suffering."

Neighbors describe her as fearless and tireless. Rosa Delgado, a mother of four who has relied on Ruiz's kitchen, called her "an angel who never sleeps."

"When my husband lost his job, Maria made sure my children ate," Delgado said. "She asked for nothing. She only gave."

## Recognition That Changed Everything

The CNN Heroes program, which honors everyday people making extraordinary differences in their communities, selected Ruiz from thousands of nominations worldwide. The award includes a financial grant to expand her charitable work — funding that Ruiz says will allow her to double the number of families she serves.

But the most emotional moment came when organizers revealed a second gift. For years, Ruiz had lived in a modest, deteriorating home with a leaking roof and no reliable plumbing, pouring every resource into others while neglecting her own needs. A coalition of donors and local builders had secretly constructed a new, custom home for her.

When Ruiz first saw the house, complete with a large kitchen designed to help her prepare community meals, she fell to her knees.

"This kitchen is not just for me," she said, smiling through tears. "Think of how many more people we can feed now."

## Looking Ahead

Despite the honors, Ruiz insists nothing about her mission will change. She was back at her community kitchen the very next morning, apron on, stirring a massive pot of soup.

"Awards are beautiful, and I am grateful," she said. "But the work is not finished. There are still hungry children in Juárez. As long as I can stand, I will serve them."

For the people of Juárez, Maria Ruiz was a hero long before the cameras arrived — and will remain one long after they leave.
